after.author_corresponding_institution: Sports Medicine Research Group, Institute for Sport and Sport Science, TU Dortmund University, Dortmund, Germany
after.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) represents a multifaceted neuroinflammatory disease for which regular exercise is now recommended by many healthcare institutions. Although preclinical studies indicate robust immunomodulatory effects of exercise, evidence from human studies is lacking. In this randomized controlled trial, persons with MS (pwMS) were assigned to three months of high-intensity interval training or a passive control condition, with outcomes assessed at baseline, after intervention, and a fourweek follow-up. Additionally, a healthy matched control group was included. Besides exercise-induced sustained increases in physical fitness, systemic inflammation was diminished and the Treg-to-TH17.1 ratio improved after exercise. Untargeted proteomic analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells covering >7000 proteins revealed an exercise-induced decrease in proteins implicated in inflammatory diseases (i.e., MTHFD2). This was supported by inferred transcription factor activity analysis, which indicated enhanced polarization of immune cells toward anti-inflammatory phenotypes at follow-up. Using flow cytometry, we identified an LFA-1highCD4+ T-cell subset that was associated with disease biomarkers and exhibited increased CCR4 expression compared to healthy matched subjects which was reduced after exercise. Our findings significantly expand knowledge of how exercise training exerts immediate and sustained immunomodulatory effects in pwMS and thereby strengthens the mechanistic rationale for exercise recommendations made by healthcare professionals.

after.authors: Aguilar-Mogas, A.; Hamilton, J. N.; Ju, A. W.; Lea, C. S.; Shelton, C. H.
after.author_corresponding_institution: East Carolina University
after.abstract: Background: Prostate cancer is the most common male cancer, and second most common cause of cancer mortality in the US. Disparities abound in this disease for reasons that need further study, including social and ethnic barriers, geographic barriers, and biological differences. North Carolina is the second largest state by rural population measures (3.5 million), which provides ample geography to study these disparities. Materials and Methods: A dataset containing all patients with a medical record documenting a diagnosis of and/or treatment for de novo prostate cancer within the mostly rural ECU Health 9-hospital system was characterized over a 20-year period for structural inequities, access barriers, and biological differences. Results: Stages and outcomes of prostate cancer changed temporally, reflecting changes in screening, treatment, and inclusion of prognostic factors such as prostate-specific antigen, Gleason score, and other factors. Late stage (4) prostate cancer disproportionately affected our system as a whole and smaller community hospitals, with higher death rates seen in community, mostly rural programs that lack access to all required components of care. Conclusion: Stages of prostate cancer changed considerably over the study period, reflecting changes in screening recommendations, and staging criteria. Late stage (4) disease increased over the analytic period, was higher than NCDB references by period, and disproportionately affected community programs where resources were sparse, correlating with worse outcomes.

after.authors: Kubit, B. M.; Asthagiri, A.; Lopez, K. L.; Wang, J.; Parrish, C.; Trebour, B.; Zhao, Z.; Yesil, D.; Toivonen, A.; Jacobowitz, A.; Quigley, B.; Wu, X.; Kim, J. C.; Large, E. W.; Loui, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Northeastern University
after.abstract: Noninvasive clinical innovations for restoring gamma activity via sound and light stimulation have the potential to improve memory and cognitive abilities in Alzheimer's disease. We assessed whether pairing music with theta- and gamma-band light changes memory-supporting neural dynamics, and whether those changes track cognition. In an ongoing randomized feasibility trial, 38 older adults with cognitive impairment completed eight weeks of an audiovisual intervention. The treatment group (n = 19) listened to self-selected music while viewing light stimulation that consisted of a 39-Hz gamma-band signal modulated by delta- and theta-band musical rhythms. The control group (n = 19) listened to podcasts while viewing synchronized lights without the gamma frequency (delta-band only). Before and after the 8-week intervention, participants completed a face-name association task and the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive (ADAS-Cog). Individuals in the treatment group showed significant improvements on a face-name association task and the ADAS-Cog. Cluster-based permutation testing showed a larger increase in phase-amplitude coupling between acoustic theta phase and frontal EEG gamma amplitude in the treatment group compared to the control group. Across participants, increases in stimulus-driven theta to EEG-gamma phase-amplitude coupling were associated with improvements in memory. These preliminary results suggest that theta-gamma stimulation delivered through music and lights strengthens cross-frequency coupling, and may correspondingly strengthen associative memory.

after.authors: Tah, S.; Cheshire, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: West Virginia University School of Medicine
after.abstract: Objective: To evaluate whether GLP-1 RA use added to statins is associated with lower all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), and ischemic stroke versus statin monotherapy in ASCVD patients with body mass index (BMI) 30 kg/m2. Approach and Results:Using the TriNetX Research Network (108 U.S. healthcare organizations), we identified ASCVD patients with BMI 30 kg/m2 on statins initiating a GLP-1 RA (n=166,278) versus statin-only controls (n=920,176). Propensity score matching on 34 covariates yielded 119,911 matched pairs followed 3 years. Prespecified analyses included a BMI 35 subgroup (62,385 pairs), four washout sensitivity analyses (30-120 days), and a familial hypercholesterolemia exclusion analysis (161,312 matched pairs). Results. GLP-1 RA use was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (4.0% vs. 7.5%; HR 0.479; 95% CI: 0.463-0.496; p<0.001), MI (HR 0.762; 95% CI: 0.737-0.788; p<0.001), and ischemic stroke (HR 0.671; 95% CI: 0.588-0.766; p<0.001). Benefits were consistent across the BMI 35 subgroup and all washout analyses. GLP-1 RA users were more likely to achieve LDL <55 mg/dL by risk analysis (17.1% vs. 15.3%; RR 1.118; p<0.001); the Kaplan-Meier analysis was non-significant (HR 1.007; p=0.538). Mortality benefit was preserved in the FH exclusion analysis. Conclusion: ASCVD patients with obesity on statins, GLP-1 RA use was associated with substantially lower mortality, MI, and stroke, suggesting GLP-1 RAs may serve as cardioprotective adjuncts to statin therapy in this population.

items.content_text:

Trial RegistrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT05506423.

after.title: Preprint: Vitamin D supplementation to prevent tuberculosis infection and disease: systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
after.authors: Jolliffe, D. A.; Middelkoop, K.; Ganmaa, D.; Irmuun, B.; Sluyter, J. D.; Sudfeld, C. R.; Fawzi, W. W.; Martineau, A. R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Queen Mary University of London
after.abstract:
BackgroundSeveral randomised controlled trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection and disease have been conducted, but no individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis has been conducted.

MethodsWe conducted a systematic review, one-stage and two-stage IPD meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420251173446) of double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of vitamin D supplementation for prevention of tuberculosis infection or disease. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to October 29, 2026. The co-primary outcomes were incident tuberculosis infection (evidenced by tuberculin skin test or Interferon Gamma Release Assay conversion) and incident tuberculosis disease. Mixed-effects models estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs), accounting for trial and prespecified covariates. Prespecified subgroup analyses investigated effect modification by sex and age, body-mass index, vitamin D status, and BCG vaccination status.

FindingsFour trials contributed IPD for 14,619 participants. Vitamin D did not reduce risk of incident tuberculosis infection (9,557 participants; aOR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81-1.18; p=0.79) or incident tuberculosis disease (14,533 participants; aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.10; p=0.15). There was no evidence of effect modification by participant characteristics investigated in sub-group analyses, including in participants with 25-hydroxyvitamin D <25 nmol/L (infection: aOR 0.95, 95% CI 0.67-1.34; disease: 1.01, 0.45-2.30). Serious adverse events and mortality were unaffected.

InterpretationVitamin D supplementation did not reduce the risk of incident tuberculosis infection or disease in the populations studied, either overall or within sub-groups. The 95% confidence interval of the effect estimate for prevention of tuberculosis disease remains compatible with a potentially important benefit, and further trials for this indication may be warranted.

after.authors: Cromie, A.; Kaur, M.; Powell, N.; Brown, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Swansea University College of Medicine: Swansea University Medical School
after.abstract:
BackgroundMedical professionals face significant work overload, with excessive job demands often strongly associated with attrition and burnout. Consequences of burnout include reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, reduced patient care, lower patient satisfaction and increased healthcare costs. UK Medical students are also at high risk of burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions are effective individual-level treatments; however, more research is required to investigate the efficacy for healthcare professionals and students.

MethodFour cohorts of second-year medical students at Cardiff University participated in a five-day, in-person mindfulness-based intervention. Pre (T1) and post (T2) intervention and follow-up (T3) survey data were collected online.

ResultsAll outcome measures saw a statistically significant improvement (N=69) post intervention, current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001); Psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up. Satisfaction ratings were consistently high, and completion rate was 100%.

DiscussionMedical schools should consider implementing mindfulness-based interventions into medical curricula, as a feasible and acceptable student selected preventative tool to address burnout and incorporate student perspectives on delivery; to prevent mental ill health in medical professionals.

after.title: Preprint: Cumulative Multidomain Vulnerability and Early Mortality After Heart Transplantation: Development and Temporal Evaluation of the RIGHT-HTx Framework
after.authors: Balakrishnan, K. R.; Kemundel Genny, S. R.; Tungatru, M.; Davidson, N.; Sahayaraj, A.; Aravind, A.; Vanga, S.; Singh, N.; Nallamuthu, N.; Jegdish, A.; Krithika, K.; Ratnagiri, R. K.; Chandrasekaran, R.; RAMASWAMY, R. K.; Manikala, V.; Kumar, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Heart and Lung Transplant & Mechanical Circulatory Support, MGM Healthcare
after.abstract:
BACKGROUNDRisk models from high-income transplant programmes may not generalise to resource-constrained settings with different recipient acuity, donor characteristics and access to mechanical circulatory support. We developed RIGHT-HTx, a parsimonious framework integrating clinical and physiological vulnerabilities, and evaluated its prognostic performance in a subsequent same-centre cohort.

METHODSThis retrospective single-centre study included 436 consecutive adult heart transplant recipients (2012- 2026). Of 357 development recipients, 341 (95.5%) were score-evaluable. RIGHT-HTx incorporated three vulnerability domains: clinical acuity (INTERMACS 1-2), graded renal dysfunction (eGFR 30- 59 or <30 mL/min/1.73 m2) and haemodynamic-donor mismatch (TPG >12 mmHg combined with donor-to-recipient weight ratio <1.0). A seven-point Cox-derived score underwent internal validation using 1,000 bootstrap resamples and was applied unchanged to 79 subsequent recipients. Low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories represented zero, one and [≥]2 affected domains, respectively.

RESULTSAmong development recipients, 75/341 (22.0%) died within one year. Mortality increased across low-, intermediate- and high-risk categories (8.1%, 20.3% and 55.6%; log-rank P<0.001). Elevated TPG was not significantly associated with mortality individually, whereas its combination with donor undersizing was independently associated with mortality (adjusted HR 2.87, 95% CI 1.53-5.40; P=0.001). The full model improved discrimination beyond renal dysfunction alone (optimism-corrected {Delta}C-index 0.067), and the simplified score achieved an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.732.

The temporal cohort more often had [≥]1 affected domain (75.9% versus 60.4%; P=0.010). Discrimination was comparable (C-index 0.738, 95% CI 0.643-0.833), although observed Kaplan- Meier one-year mortality exceeded original predictions (35.4% versus 25.4%; calibration slope 0.929). In pooled analyses (n=420), mortality increased from 8.4% (13/154) with no affected domain to 57.3% (47/82) with two or more.

CONCLUSIONSRIGHT-HTx identifies cumulative multidomain vulnerability associated with early mortality after heart transplantation. Temporal discrimination was comparable, but absolute-risk calibration differed. The framework may support risk recognition and mitigation, not transplant eligibility or allocation; independent multicentre validation is required before clinical implementation.

after.authors: pious, I. S.; Beyeza-Kashesya, J.; Namagembe, I.; Twesigemukama, S.; Godfrey James, A.; Saad Sessimba, K.; Balikudembe, K.; Andrew, B.; Mary, M.; Mwanje, D.; Musanje, K.; Sekikubo, M.

after.abstract:
BackgroundThe Copper-T intrauterine device (Cu-T IUD) is a highly effective, non- hormonal, long-acting reversible contraceptive that can protect against pregnancy for up to 12 years, with a failure rate under 1%. Despite its clinical efficacy, early discontinuation remains a substantial challenge in Uganda, where discontinuation is approximated at 29% within the first year of use. Understanding the experiences of women using the Cu-T IUD is important to predict factors associated with discontinuation and to inform practice.

MethodsBetween September and November 2025, we conducted twenty in-depth interviews with women of reproductive age (15-49 years) who had used a Cu-T IUD for at least two years, recruited from the family planning clinic of Kawempe National Referral Hospital, Kampala, Uganda. Data were analysed thematically, guided by the Social-Ecological Model and Lazarus and Folkmans Transactional Model of Stress and Coping.

ResultsLong-term Cu-T IUD users reported both positive and negative experiences shaped by individual, interpersonal, and community factors. Two themes were identified at the individual-level domain: experiences during insertion and post-insertion experiences. Negative experiences, particularly heavy menstrual bleeding, anxiety, and abdominal pain, were common and distressing. Participants employed coping strategies, including taking painkillers, using home remedies, and resting, to manage these challenges with Cu-T IUD use.

ConclusionsNegative experiences of Cu-T IUD are common among long-term users; womens coping strategies such as taking painkillers lead to continued use. Client-centred pre- insertion counselling addressing both anticipated side effects and common misconceptions, alongside accessible follow-up services, may facilitate long-term Cu-T IUD use.

after.authors: Pedersen, T. J.; Yu, J.; Li, A.; Ibanez, L.; Bubu, O. M.; Lucey, B. P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Minnesota Medical School
after.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-{beta} plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of tau. Suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist, was previously shown to acutely reduce the ratio of phosphorylated tau-181 to unphosphorylated tau-181 (pT181/T181) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). However, its effects on plasma pT181/T181 and broader proteomic networks remain unknown. Here, we conducted a secondary analysis of samples from a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 25 participants receiving placebo or suvorexant 20 mg. Paired CSF and plasma samples were collected longitudinally via indwelling intrathecal and intravenous catheters. Plasma AD biomarkers were quantified by mass spectrometry, and proteomic profiling was performed using the SomaScan 11K assay on samples from hours 0, 16, and 24. after.authors: Turkulainen, E.; Arvas, M.; Koskinen, M.; Ilmakunnas, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Finnish Red Cross Blood Service
after.abstract:
BACKGROUNDPreoperative prediction of red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in elective surgery serves two complementary purposes: enabling patient blood management (PBM) interventions before surgery and supporting blood product supply planning for elective lists. Beyond patient risk factors, individual surgeon practice may also contribute to transfusion rates, but this effect has not been fully quantified.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODSIn a retrospective cohort of 279,905 elective surgical procedures at Helsinki University Hospital (2021-2025), we trained four gradient-boosted tree (CatBoost) models crossing patient factors with procedure group and pseudonymised surgeon identity. All predictors were restricted to data available seven or more days before scheduled surgery. The primary outcome was any allogeneic RBC transfusion from operating-room entry through seven postoperative days. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) on a held-out 20% test set. Surgeon-level effects were characterised by Shapley additive explanation (SHAP) values.

RESULTSThe transfusion rate was 2.2%. The patient-only model achieved AUPRC 0.261 (no-skill baseline 0.022). Adding surgeon identity to the procedure-adjusted model increased AUPRC from 0.440 to 0.472 (+0.032; 95% CI 0.020-0.044), raising lift from 20.3 to 21.7. Surgeon identity was the third most important of 72 features by permutation importance.

DISCUSSIONThe operating surgeon was associated with RBC transfusion beyond patient and procedure factors, and surgeon identity was the third most important predictor in a deployment-realistic model using only data available a week before surgery. This information is readily available from routine records and could support PBM audit and blood supply planning for elective surgery.

after.title: Preprint: Uncovering Distinct Phenotypes of Early Onset Heart Failure in Women
after.authors: Khorsandi, J.; Yu, Y.; Tinnium, D.; Ganesh, S.; Alahapphan, R.; Oyinloye, P.; Mueller, K.; Ardekani, S.; Taylor, C. O.; Greenstein, J. L.; Ndumele, C. E.; Michos, E. D.; Bairey Merz, C. N.; Barrett, R. B.; Minhas, A. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
after.abstract:
BackgroundHeart failure in younger women is understudied and may reflect heterogeneous pathways and risk not adequately captured by conventional classifications. We aimed to identify clinically distinct phenotypes of early-onset heart failure in women, assess their prognostic significance, and evaluate their transportability in an independent national cohort.

MethodsWe identified women aged 18-55 years with heart failure using electronic health record data from a large multi-hospital system. A variational deep embedding model incorporating 283 clinical features was used for unsupervised phenotyping. Associations with subsequent inpatient hospitalization, emergency department utilization, and mortality were evaluated using age-stratified Cox models. Phenotype transportability was assessed by both applying the institutionally trained model and by independent de novo clustering as a replication analysis in the All of Us cohort.

ResultsAmong 1,407 young women with heart failure (median age, 45 years), four phenotypes were identified: hypertensive pregnancy (n=494), cardiorenal (n=276), autoimmune (n=394), and cardiometabolic-ischemic (n=243), with a bootstrap adjusted Rand index of 0.65 and silhouette score of 0.45. Compared with the hypertensive pregnancy phenotype, risks of inpatient hospitalization were highest for the cardiorenal (HR 2.86 [95% CI, 2.35-3.49]) and autoimmune (HR 2.25 [95% CI, 1.87-2.70]) phenotypes; mortality risks were similarly elevated (HR 4.65 [95% CI, 3.17-6.82] and HR 4.38 [95% CI, 3.03-6.31], respectively) in these two groups. In All of Us participants (n=682), transferred phenotypes retained their principal clinical characteristics and continued to stratify hospitalization risk. Independent clustering most strongly reproduced the cardiorenal phenotype (Jaccard index, 0.744).

ConclusionsEarly-onset heart failure in women comprises distinct cardio-obstetric, cardiorenal, autoimmune, and cardiometabolic-ischemic phenotypes with divergent clinical outcomes. These findings support a life-course approach to heart failure classification in women that complements conventional frameworks and incorporates pregnancy history and female-predominant systemic conditions.

Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSUnsupervised machine learning identifies distinct clinical phenotypes of heart failure among young women, highlighting heterogeneity in a population that remains understudied.
These phenotypes captured differing cardiometabolic, cardiovascular, and pregnancy-related characteristics, suggesting potentially distinct pathways contributing to heart failure development.
External validation in the All of Us cohort supported external validity and demonstrated the potential for identifying these patterns across diverse healthcare populations.


What Are the Clinical Implications?Heart failure in young women is clinically diverse, underscoring the importance of comprehensive assessment beyond traditional heart failure classifications, including cardiometabolic risk factors and pregnancy history.
Recognition of distinct clinical phenotypes may help clinicians identify women with differing risk profiles and inform more individualized approaches to cardiovascular evaluation, risk factor management, and longitudinal follow-up.
Further studies are needed to determine whether phenotypes differ in treatment responses and whether phenotype-guided management can improve outcomes.

after.title: Preprint: Community health workers experiences with a digital clinical decision support system for longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho: a mixed-methods study
after.authors: Gerber, F.; Raeber, F.; Moruthoane, M.; Khaemba, A.; Bhandari, N.; Kunwar, L.; Sanchez-Samaniego, G.; Gupta, R.; Williams, A.; Tahirsylaj, T.; Mathulise, M.; Kabi, T.; Mokaeane, M.; Maphenchane, M.; Molulela, M.; Khomolishoele, M.; Sematle, M. P.; Sao, L.; Tlahali, M.; Shankar, U.; Basler, D. B.; Kindler, K.; Grimm, P.; Labhardt, N. D.; Amstutz, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University Hospital Basel
after.abstract:
Community health workers (CHWs) are increasingly delivering chronic care in resource-constrained settings but require support to manage complex longitudinal clinical workflows. In the Community-Based chronic Care Lesotho (ComBaCaL) project in rural Lesotho, CHWs provide longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care, supported by the ComBaCaL Community Health Toolkit (CHT) application. The application combines longitudinal participant management and task coordination with clinical decision support for screening, diagnosis, treatment initiation and adjustment, cardiovascular risk management, referral, and follow-up for hypertension and diabetes care. This model of care has demonstrated improved or maintained clinical outcomes compared to facility-based care only. We conducted a mixed-methods study among all 103 participating CHWs to evaluate their experiences with the application.

All CHWs completed a 38-item questionnaire, and 22 participated in qualitative interviews or focus group discussions. Overall usability was high, with a mean System Usability Scale score of 75.6 (SD 13.0), and 98 (95%) CHWs were satisfied or very satisfied with the application. General application functions and diagnosis and treatment tasks were rated easy or very easy by 98% of participants. The most frequently reported benefits were task reminders (92%), structured clinical guidance (87%), overview of allocated participants (81%), and retention of participant information (81%). Main challenges were lengthy questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, and limited internet connectivity. Qualitative findings showed that ease of use increased with experience, supported by training and supervision. Participants described how algorithmic guidance and task reminders supported care delivery, while also identifying tensions between standardized workflows and flexibility in day-to-day care.

The ComBaCaL CHT application was highly usable and valued by CHWs. High perceived usability extended from general application functions to complex clinical workflows. CHT demonstrated suitability as a configurable framework for implementing such context-specific workflows for hypertension and diabetes care when accompanied by appropriate workflow design, training, and supervision.

Author summaryHigh blood pressure and diabetes require repeated follow-up and treatment decisions, which is difficult where healthcare professionals are scarce. Community health workers (CHWs) may help expand access to this care, but they need appropriate tools to manage complex clinical tasks. We evaluated a digital application designed to support CHWs in delivering hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho. Overall, 103 CHWs used an application built with the Community Health Toolkit to support hypertension and diabetes care. The application helped manage participants and follow-up tasks and provided step-by-step guidance for screening, diagnosis, treatment, referral, and repeated care visits. All 103 CHWs completed a survey, and 22 participated in interviews or focus group discussions.

CHWs found the application easy to use and useful for their work. Frequently reported benefits included reminders, procedural guidance, better participant oversight, and retention of participant information over time. Ease of use improved with experience and was supported by training and supervision. Challenges included lengthy research questionnaires, difficulties charging tablets, limited internet connectivity, and standardized digital workflows that did not fit day-to-day circumstances.

Our findings show that a configurable open-source digital application can support CHWs in delivering complex, longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in a remote rural setting.

after.authors: Kadali, N.; UPPALURI, K. R.; Challa, H. J.; Vempati, K. K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: GenepoweRx
after.abstract: Background. Low-coverage plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is an inexpensive substrate for cancer detection. Standard pipelines discard fragments with low mapping quality, which originate mostly from repetitive DNA, although pericentromeric satellite repeats are frequently hypomethylated in cancer. We asked whether the fraction of multi-mapping cfDNA fragments differs between early-stage cancer and matched healthy controls, and how it compares with conventional fragmentomic features under strict control of technical factors. Methods. We analysed public plasma cfDNA whole-genome sequencing from 25 patients with stage I to III breast cancer and 25 healthy controls matched 1:1 for age, sex, smoking and alcohol use, each pair processed in the same library and sequencing batch, and from 8 early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cases with 8 matched controls. For every sample we computed the fraction of autosomal fragments with MAPQ < 30 and the share of these fragments located in centromeric and heterochromatic cytobands, and related them to stage, grade and copy-number deviation as proxies of tumour burden. Classifiers were evaluated by leave-one-pair-out cross-validation in breast cancer and, trained on breast cancer only, applied unchanged to HCC. Robustness to GC content and sequencing depth was tested by within-fold residualisation and by fragment-level GC weighting. Conventional fragmentomic features (fragment length, end motifs, copy number, DELFI-like profiles and window features at transcription start sites) were evaluated under four GC-handling analyses. Results. The multi-mapping fraction was higher in breast cancer than in matched controls (median 5.38 % vs 5.19 %; higher in 19/25 pairs; paired p = 0.0006; cross-validated AUC 0.81, 95 % CI 0.67 - 0.94), in stage I (9/10 pairs), stage II (7/10) and stage III (3/5) disease and in every sequencing batch. The excess was concentrated in centromeric and heterochromatic bands, whose share of multi-mapping fragments rose from 22.0 % to 23.4 % (19/25 pairs; p = 0.004). Both signals persisted after within-fold adjustment for GC content and/or depth (AUC 0.64 - 0.76 for the multi-mapping fraction, 0.71 - 0.76 for the heterochromatic share) and under fragment-level GC weighting (18/25 pairs; p = 0.003). The multi-mapping difference was largest in stage I and decreased with stage (Spearman {rho} = -0.42, p = 0.04), and neither feature was associated with grade or copy-number deviation. In public tissue methylomes, satellites were hypomethylated in breast tumours to a similar extent as other late-replicating DNA, but the bin-level association between tumour hypomethylation and the cfDNA excess was weak and was explained by GC content. In HCC, the pre-specified endpoint, the breast-trained multi-mapping model, was not met (AUC 0.73; 5/8 pairs; sign test p = 0.36). In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-specified, the heterochromatic share was higher in 7/8 HCC pairs (p = 0.016; locked AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.62 - 1.00); across all 33 pairs, including the discovery pairs, it was higher in the cancer case in 26 (post hoc sign test p = 0.0007). In contrast, conventional fragmentomic features reached AUC 0.71 (breast) and 0.77 (HCC) only without fragment-level GC control; they tracked the per-sample coverage GC dependence and fell to chance under each of three GC-controlled analyses, including one that preserves promoter-specific signal. Conclusions. Multi-mapping cfDNA fragments, which are routinely discarded, differed between early-stage breast cancer and batch-matched controls, largely independently of GC content and sequencing depth, with an excess in centromeric and heterochromatic DNA. The signal did not scale with stage, its biological origin is unproven, and a read-quality contribution cannot be excluded from fragment files. It is a candidate marker that requires confirmation in larger cohorts with raw reads and tumour-fraction estimates.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Boston Children Hospital (Harvard Medical School)
after.abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

after.title: Preprint: Additional tuberculosis case detection through repeat household contact investigation at 6 and 12 months: a retrospective cohort study in Kasama, a peri-urban district in Zambia
after.authors: Mwaba, P. B.; Mukupa, M.; Sakala, J.; Mwaba, I.; Siameka, D.; Maimbolwa, M. M.; Chanda, C.; Mputu, M.; Zimba, K. M.; Kasese-Chanda, N.; Chimzizi, R.; Mubanga, A.; Muyoyeta, M.; Kagujje, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: CIDRZ: Center for Infectious Disease Research in Zambia
after.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis contact investigation (TBCI) facilitates early detection of TB among household contacts. However, evidence on the additional contribution of repeat TBCI in high-burden settings remains limited. We assessed the contribution of repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months to TB case detection in Kasama District, Zambia.   Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort analysis of routinely collected programme data from five purposively selected high-volume TB diagnostic facilities. Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients notified between January 2023 and April 2024 underwent symptom-based TB screening at baseline and at 6 and 12 months. We estimated round-specific TB detection yields, the cumulative proportion diagnosed with TB, and the contribution of repeat investigations to overall case detection.   Results: Among 1,250 index TB patients, 3,648 household contacts were identified and screened at baseline. TB was diagnosed in 143 (3.9%) contacts at baseline, 31 (0.9%) at month 6, and 25 (0.7%) at month 12. Overall, 199 (5.5%) contacts were diagnosed with TB across the three screening rounds, of whom 159 (79.9%) had bacteriologically confirmed disease. Repeat investigations identified 56 additional cases, representing 28.1% of all TB diagnoses.   Conclusions: Repeat TBCI at 6 and 12 months identified additional TB cases beyond baseline screening, although detection yields declined across successive rounds. These findings support further evaluation of risk-based follow-up strategies and more sensitive baseline screening approaches to optimize TB case detection and resource utilization in high-burden settings.

after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Pennsylvania
after.abstract: Objectives: HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer is rising, yet the natural history of oral-HPV, particularly persistence remains poorly characterized in sub-Saharan Africa and in people living with HIV (PLWH). We characterized oral HPV prevalence, incident detection, persistence, and clearance over four visits in a Nigerian mother-youth cohort with and without HIV and quantified the genotype distribution relative to vaccine coverage. Methods: Within the prospective HOMINY cohort, 1075 participants (404 mothers and 671 youth) were followed across four visits at 6-month intervals. Oral rinses were genotyped with the Seegene Allplex HPV28 assay (28 genotypes). Persistence was defined as detection at [≥]2 visit (not necessarily consecutive), with type-specific and visit 2-4 sensitivity definitions. We used modified-Poisson models for visit-level detection, Markov multistate models for acquisition and clearance, and a permutation test for mother-youth genotype concordance. Results: Oral HPV was detected at least once in 112 participants (10.4% overall; 11.1% mothers and 10% youth); incident detection was around 6% in both groups. Persistence was uncommon (1.9%), and only 3 had oral HPV DNA detected at all four visits. Clearance predominated across every visit interval. In Markov models, clearance was slower in PLWH (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22-0.77) with no difference in acquisition (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.5). Persistence concentrated among PLWH. Only 31.2% of ever-positive participants carried a Gardasil-9 preventable strain of HPV; HPV16 and HPV39 were most frequent. Mother-youth genotype concordance exceeded chance (permutation p =0.009). Conclusion: Oral HPV was common but transient; persistence was confined to a small PLWH minority and was dominated by high-risk non-vaccine genotypes, leaving most infections beyond the reach of current vaccines.

after.title: Preprint: EIN-RECAP: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Summarization and Retrieval of Infectious-Disease Expert Discussions
after.authors: Choudhuri, A.; Zhong, Y.; Beekmann, S.; Hodges, J.; Jha, K.; Segre, A. M.; Adhikari, B.; Polgreen, P. M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The University of Iowa
after.abstract: Infectious disease experts exchange practical knowledge through clinical discussions, but identifying relevant information across years of conversations is difficult. These discussions often contain differing opinions and emerging observations that are not yet reflected in published evidence. We present EIN-RECAP, an AI-assisted platform developed with Emerging Infections Network (EIN) experts and deployed in beta to summarize and search historical discussions. The system combines retrieval-grounded summarization, citation validation, and hybrid search while distinguishing published evidence from community experience. We evaluated summarization methods across 3,185 threads and conducted blinded expert review on a recent subset. Although a multi-agent workflow achieved stronger automated scores, experts favored a simpler generation pipeline and identified repetition, inaccuracies, and overconfident recommendations in the more complex system. This feedback motivated an ensemble that improved discussion coverage and key clinical points on nine high-disagreement threads, although retrieval relevance remained a limitation. Our findings demonstrate the importance of expert involvement in clinical AI development and show why automated evaluation alone is insufficient to guide system selection.

after.authors: Murad, B.; Campello Jorge, C. A.; George, G. C.; Queiroz, I.; Karnam, Y.; Spahlinger, G.; Hofmann Bowman, M. A.; Burris, N. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Wisconsin-Madison
after.abstract: Background: Ascending aortic surveillance relies on diameter thresholds, yet most dissections occur below them. Inflammation drives aortic wall remodeling independent of diameter. Inflammation drives aortic wall remodeling independent of diameter. Inflammatory indices derived from routine blood counts, such as neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), red cell distribution width (RDW), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) have been show to predict adverse cardiovascular outcomes, but their association with ascending aortic growth is unclear. Methods and Results: We retrospectively studied adults with 2 computed tomography (CT) scans of the native ascending aorta 6 months apart at a single center (2000-2023), excluding those with aortitis or no complete blood count during follow-up. Markers were summarized as 95th percentile values per patient and per scan interval. Growth was defined as a 2-mm increase in mid-ascending aortic diameter. Patient-level logistic regression and interval-level generalized estimating equation models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, baseline diameter, systolic blood pressure, diabetes, and heritable thoracic aortic disease. Among 3,262 patients, data were available in 1,882 for RDW, 1,471 for NLR, and 1,468 for SII; 192 (10.2%) met criteria for growth. Only RDW was independently associated with growth in the overall cohort (patient level: odds ratio [OR] 1.071, 95% CI 1.002-1.144, p=0.043; interval level: OR 1.075, 95% CI 1.012-1.141, p=0.019); NLR (p=0.080) and SII (p=0.164) were not. Among patients with guideline-defined ascending aortic dilation (40 mm), all three markers were associated with interval growth (RDW OR 1.14, NLR OR 1.05, SII OR 1.01 per 100 units; all p 0.014), whereas none were among aortas <40 mm; effect modification was significant for NLR (p=0.01). Conclusions: RDW was modestly associated with ascending aortic growth overall, and all three markers were associated with interval growth in patients with guideline-defined aortic dilation, suggesting that systemic inflammation may contribute to progression of aortic dilation. Prospective studies with more specific inflammatory markers are needed.

after.title: Preprint: Late-Stage Concentration of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Burden in US Adults: Disability-Adjusted Life Years Across AHA Stages, 2005 to 2023
after.authors: Wang, X.; Qiao, Y.; Sun, H.; Wang, Y.; Zhou, H.; Zhang, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Beijing University of Chinese Medicine Dongfang Hospital
after.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular prevention is increasingly prioritised using burden estimates, yet disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) reward late-stage treatment by construction. Whether that bias is large for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, and where the population is accumulating relative to where the burden sits, is unknown. Methods: We pooled nine National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycles (2005-2023) and assigned CKM stages 0-4 from measured blood pressure, adiposity, glycaemia, lipids, kidney function, urine albumin, self-reported cardiovascular disease, and 10-year PREVENT risk. Years lived with disability used GBD disability weights. Years of life lost combined national death counts, stage-specific mortality from linked mortality files (1999-2018), and period life tables. A second aim attributed burden to smoking and physical inactivity, two exposures outside the CKM definition. Results: In 2021-2023, 13.8% of adults were stage 0, 21.3% stage 1, 49.1% stage 2, 6.5% stage 3, and 9.3% stage 4. CKM accounted for 20.0 million DALYs annually (7,881 age-standardised per 100,000), of which 4.1 million were YLD and 15.9 million attributable YLL. Stages 3-4, 15.8% of adults, generated 76% of attributable YLL; stage 4 alone generated 65% of YLD and 49% of attributable YLL. Adjusted mortality rose from stage 2 (hazard ratio 1.39) through stage 4 (3.22), while stage 1 did not differ from stage 0 (0.99; 95% CI, 0.78-1.25). Between 2006 and 2016, stage 0 prevalence fell 2.3% per year and stage 1 rose 3.1% per year. Smoking and physical inactivity accounted for 30.5% of burden (95% CI, 25.7-35.1). Conclusions: CKM burden is concentrated in stages 3-4, where excess mortality begins, while the population has been shifting into stage 1, where mortality is normal. DALY-based prioritisation will therefore systematically underfund the stage in which the next generation of patients is being created.

after.authors: Ndhlovu, S.; Zhang, D. S.; Li, L.; Liu, Z.
after.author_corresponding_institution: NYU Grossman Long Island School of Medicine
after.abstract: Introduction: Studies have shown a high prevalence of mental health problems among immigrants, but findings for their children are mixed. We examined the association between parental nativity and mental health among U.S. adolescents and assessed whether these associations varied by sex and race/ethnicity. Methods: We analyzed pooled cross-sectional data from the 2022-2024 National Health Interview Survey, including 12,540 adolescents aged 12-17 years. The exposure was parental nativity. The outcomes were adolescents' mental health, including anxiety, depression, behavioral difficulties, and peer relationships. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and nearest neighbor matching were used to control confounders. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to estimate the association between parent nativity and each outcome. Subgroup analyses were conducted by sex and race/ethnicity. Results: Compared with adolescents with U.S.-born parents, adolescents with at least one foreign-born parent had lower odds of anxiety (Odds Ratio [OR]=0.62, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.54-0.71), depression (OR=0.71, 95% CI: 0.60-0.84), and behavioral difficulties (OR=0.56, 95% CI: 0.43-0.72), but not relationship difficulties (OR=0.97, 95% CI: 0.74-1.26), in the IPTW analysis. Findings from nearest-neighbor matching were consistent. In exploratory stratified analyses, inverse associations were observed among Hispanic adolescents and adolescents classified as other race/ethnicity. Conclusion: Parental nativity was associated with adolescent mental health, with adolescents of at least one foreign-born parent showing lower odds of anxiety, depression, and behavioral difficulties. Future studies are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and identify protective factors that help inform interventions to promote adolescent mental health.

after.title: Preprint: Epidemiological Modeling of Seasonal Influenza Through Periodic Mean-Reverting Stochastic Processes
after.authors: Mostafa, F.; Allen, L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Arizona State University
after.abstract: Seasonal influenza follows annual cycles, but variation in epidemic magnitude and timing complicates preparedness. We applied periodic mean reverting stochastic differential equations (SDEs) to seven seasons of weekly Texas influenza surveillance data. Missing observations were imputed using MissForest and compared with four alternative methods. Stochastic variability was modeled using {sigma}X(t) dW(t), with p = 1/2,2/3,5/6, and 1, representing square root, intermediate sublinear, and multiplicative diffusion. Each specification was evaluated for direct influenza modeling and within a susceptible, exposed, infectious , and recovered model incorporating waning immunity, where the SDE governed transmission. Parameters were estimated using least squares and approximate maximum likelihood for direct models and sample-proportion weighted least squares for stochastic SEIR models. Model-based parametric bootstrap assessed direct-model parameter uncertainty. For direct modeling, p = 1/2 achieved the lowest RMSE (712.8) and AIC (5383.0), with similar AIC for p = 2/3 (5383.2). For stochastic SEIR modeling, p = 1 achieved the lowest RMSE (0.02926), compared with 0.03506 for p = 1/2. The deterministic SEIR model yielded R = 1.158. Transmission peaked approximately 10 weeks before infectious prevalence, while stochastic transmission generated variation in epidemic peak timing. Bootstrap analysis identified dependence between mean-reversion and diffusion parameters. Overall, the appropriate diffusion structure depended on the epidemiological quantity modeled, supporting flexible characterization of seasonal transmission variability while requiring prospective validation before operational forecasting.

after.title: Preprint: The cognitive profile of the schizophrenia-associated 3q29 deletion syndrome and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome
after.authors: Pollak, R. M.; Bishop, D. V.; Harner, M. K.; Khan, A.; Purcell, J. R.; Wheeler, M.; Irving, T.; Moore, T. M.; Ruparel, K.; Gur, R. C.; Gur, R. E.; Mulle, J. G.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Rutgers University
after.abstract: 3q29 deletion syndrome (3q29del) and the reciprocal 3q29 duplication syndrome (3q29dup) are associated with a range of neuropsychiatric phenotypes, including impaired cognition. However, previous sample sizes have been small, and cognitive performance has not been systematically compared between 3q29del and 3q29dup. For both disorders, the impact of familial background on cognition is unknown. 3q29del is associated with high risk for schizophrenia; in the general population individuals at Clinical High Risk (CHR) for psychosis exhibit impaired cognition, but the relationship between CHR status and cognition in 3q29del is unexplored. Here we address these questions in the largest sample of 3q29del and 3q29dup ever evaluated. Individuals with 3q29del (n=103, 58.3% male), 3q29dup (n=38, 55.3% male), and controls (n=54, 42.6% male) were assessed with the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, 5th Edition (PPVT-5) and the Penn Computerized Neurocognitive Battery (Penn-CNB). Total PPVT-5 scores and global, domain-level, and task-level Penn-CNB scores were compared across groups. Compared to controls, 3q29del participants scored an average of 24.6 and 22.9 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB, respectively (p<3E-16); 3q29dup participants scored an average of 18.8 and 14.2 points lower on the PPVT and Penn CNB (p<4E-6). In addition, 3q29del and 3q29dup exhibit unique profiles of cognitive deficits. To assess the impact of familial background on cognition, we evaluated unaffected relatives of 3q29del (n=140, 38.6% male), 3q29dup (n=25, 24.0% male), and controls (n=45, 11.1% male). The average familial shift on the Penn-CNB was 22.4 points for 3q29del and 16.7 points for 3q29 dup. Individuals with 3q29del+CHR exhibited greater cognitive deficits than 3q29del-CHR. These results demonstrate that both 3q29del and 3q29dup are associated with significant cognitive impairment and indicate that cognitive testing should be standard of care for individuals diagnosed with 3q29del or 3q29dup.

after.title: Preprint: Determinants of Prehospital Management of Superficial Burns in Pediatric Patients at Health Facilities in Mazabuka District: A Cross-Sectional Study
after.authors: KASOMA, D.; Rosen, H. E.; Machona, P. K.; Jacobs, C.; Musonda, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: UNZA
after.abstract: Background Burn injuries in children are common in low-resource settings, yet little is known about how they are managed before reaching health facilities in Zambia. Early care at home plays a key role in recovery, but harmful practices are still widely used. We examined how caregivers manage superficial burns in children and identified factors linked to good prehospital care in Mazabuka District. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study between September and December 2025 among 337 caregivers of children aged 0-15 years presenting with superficial burns. The study was conducted at three health facilities in Mazabuka District. Data were collected using structured interviews and clinical records. Prehospital burn care was classified as good or poor based on the recommended first-aid practices. Associations were assessed using Firth penalised logistic regression, and results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Only 13.1% (44/337) of caregivers provided good prehospital burn care. Urban residence was associated with lower odds of good management (AOR 0.22; 95% CI: 0.05-0.92; p=0.038). Older caregiver age reduced the odds of good care (AOR 0.92; 95% CI: 0.86-0.98; p=0.011), while increasing child age improved it (AOR 1.25; 95% CI: 1.10-1.43; p<0.001). Longer time to reach a facility was also associated with poorer care (AOR 0.96; 95% CI 0.94-0.98; p<0.001). Conclusion Good prehospital burn care was uncommon. It was associated with time to the health facility, caregiver age, child age, and urban versus rural residence, rather than with proximity to a facility alone. Programmes should promote cooling with running water, avoidance of harmful home applications, and prompt care-seeking. Messages in routine child health services may reach caregivers of young children; additional approaches are needed for older caregivers and urban communities.

after.authors: Sato, K.; Niimi, Y.; IHARA, R.; Suzuki, K.; Iwata, A.; Iwatsubo, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Tokyo Hospital
after.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Web-based registries support remote cognitive assessment for Alzheimer's disease research, but participant-driven reassessment raises questions about long-term data yield and interpretation of repeated scores. We evaluated data contribution, selective observation, and retest-dependent estimates of cognitive change in the Japanese Trial-Ready Cohort (J-TRC) Webstudy. METHODS: We analyzed over six years of J-TRC Webstudy data (launched October 2019; registrations through March 31, 2025; assessments through May 31, 2026). We examined data contribution, inactivity, reactivation, score-associated observation, first-exposure contrasts, and sensitivity to retest models and estimators. RESULTS: Among 14,912 registered accounts, 10,863 participants were eligible; 10,645 (98.0%) completed the Cognitive Function Instrument (CFI), 6,419 (59.1%) completed Cogstate, and 5,792 (53.3%) contributed assessments on multiple days. Among those with sufficient opportunity, 19.4% and 14.1% contributed data at or beyond three and five years. After 365 days without assessment, the estimated probability of resuming within two years was 7.2%. Worse prior cognitive scores were associated with lower odds of subsequent assessment (adjusted odds ratios per standard deviation: CFI, 0.952; Cogstate, 0.845). By assessment 12, returnee changes were +0.43 and +1.14 favorable baseline standard deviations (CFI, Cogstate), versus -0.06 and +0.08 in first-exposure contrasts. Marginal CFI time estimates differed under categorical versus flexible retest adjustment (+0.080 versus -0.227 standard deviations/year). DISCUSSION: High initial completion was accompanied by limited long-term data contribution. Subsequent assessment was associated with prior scores, and estimated time trends varied by retest model. Reporting assessment histories and testing model sensitivity are important for interpreting repeated online cognitive scores.

after.title: Preprint: Cognitive Performance in Prodromal Neuronal α Synuclein Disease
after.authors: Anis, S.; Zimmerman, E.; Sperling, S. A.; Alberts, J. L.; Weintraub, D.; Simuni, T.; Siderowf, A.; Fernandez, H. H.; on behalf of the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative,
after.author_corresponding_institution: Cleveland Clinic
after.abstract: Importance: Cognitive abnormalities may emerge during prodromal neuronal a-synuclein disease (NSD), but their domain specificity and longitudinal course are uncertain. Objective: To characterize baseline cognition and longitudinal change in prodromal NSD compared with healthy controls, NSD-negative genetic carriers, and sporadic Parkinson disease (PD). Design: Longitudinal cohort study using Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) data, with first visits from July 2010 through April 2026 and up to 4 years of follow-up. Setting: Multicenter cohort. Participants: Healthy controls (HC; n=244), GBA1 or LRRK2 nonmanifesting carriers without NSD (n=323), prodromal NSD participants recruited through hyposmia or isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder cohorts (n=1640), and sporadic PD (n=824). Exposures: NSD status and clinical cohort. Main Outcomes and Measures: Cognitive summary scores for verbal memory, executive function, processing speed, language, and visuospatial function, and PPMI-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE {varepsilon}4 status. Results: Among 3031 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.6 [7.0] years; 1322 female [43.6%]), prodromal NSD participants had lower baseline verbal-memory performance than HC (adjusted difference, -0.20 SD; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.07; adjusted P = .007); NSD-negative genetic carriers did not differ from HC. No other cognitive domain was lower than HC at baseline or longitudinally. In the primary age-adjusted analysis, verbal-memory trajectory differed from HC over 4 years (P = .009), whereas in a smaller age-matched sensitivity subset through year 3, it did not (P = .62); the baseline difference persisted (adjusted difference, -0.28 SD; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.10; P = .003). Adjusted MCI probability increased from 10.2% to 15.1% in prodromal NSD, compared with 8.4% to 5.0% in HC and 13.4% to 17.7% in PD. The increase was greater than in HC (ratio of annual odds ratios, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.58; adjusted P = .04) but not PD (P = .62). Conclusions and Relevance: Prodromal NSD was associated with modestly lower verbal memory and increasing MCI probability relative to HC, without lower performance in other cognitive domains. The baseline verbal-memory difference was robust, whereas the longitudinal trajectory finding was not reproduced in the smaller age-matched sensitivity subset.

after.title: Preprint: Benchmarking Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Exome Sequencing of 67 Multiple Myeloma Cell Lines
after.authors: Pugalenthi, L. S.; Nanduri, R.; Hong, R.; Ylagan, M.; Prasad, R.; Arasappan, D.; Kowalski-Muegge, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Oncology, Dell Medical School, University of Texas at Austin
after.abstract: Background. Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Similar to personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results. Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA's unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer's output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA's unfiltered output and Delly's output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA's filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions. As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools' output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

Eleven were associated with relational reports individually; entered together, only three retained independent associations surviving false discovery rate correction: cross-domain psychiatric symptom burden (beta = 0.38), delay discounting (beta = -0.11), and orienting sensitivity (beta = 0.10). To our knowledge, this is the first peer-reviewed study linking delay discounting to maternal relational reports. Depression, anxiety, anger, perceived stress, and negative affect fell to non-significance, and the symptom composite that displaced them contains none of those domains, indicating that breadth of psychiatric symptoms, not their type, tracked relational reports. A person-centered analysis converged: the latent profile with the poorest relational reports was defined by symptoms across multiple domains rather than by elevated stress alone. Associations varied across family contexts, though because each context used a different relational instrument, differences cannot be attributed to child age. These cross-sectional findings suggest that the psychological dimension most closely tied to maternal relational reports is broader than the perinatal mood constructs around which research and screening are organized, and that cross-domain symptom assessment warrants prospective evaluation as a complement to mood screening.

after.authors: Viljamaa, A.; Baumgartner, R.; Strandberg, R.; Sterner, J.; Drejian, S.; Aghayan, D.; Fernandez Moro, C.; Sparrelid, E.; Osterlund, P.; Edwin, B.; Fretland, A. A.; Geyer, N.; Engstrand, J.; Gerling, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Clinical Science, Intervention and Technology, Division of Surgery and Oncology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden
after.abstract: Introduction: Treatment strategies for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM) are increasingly complex, driving interest in advanced prognostic tools. Externally validated benchmarks based on established clinical risk scores are needed to contextualise emerging models. However, existing scores remain difficult to apply and compare, because they provide categorical risk strata rather than individualised probabilities, and because model parameters are rarely published. Here, we validate and recalibrate seven established risk scores to derive individualised recurrence probabilities for future score benchmarking. Method: Patients undergoing index CRLM resection from two tertiary centres were included: Karolinska University Hospital (retrospective KaroLiver cohort [2013-2021, follow-up to 2025, n=709]) and Oslo University Hospital (OSLO-COMET trial cohort [2012-2016, follow-up to 2022, n=198]). Performance of the GAME, m-CS, Fong, Nordlinger, Nagashima, Konopke and Helsinki scores was assessed using recurrence-free survival as the primary outcome. Results: Among 709 patients in KaroLiver (median age 67 years [IQR 59-74]; 434 men [61%]), 422 (60%) had synchronous metastases and 444 (63%) received neoadjuvant chemotherapy. All scores significantly stratified recurrence risk (log-rank P<0.001; time-dependent AUC 0.63-0.74 at 3 years), albeit with performance differences across time points. Recalibrated models showed good agreement between predicted and observed recurrence and were externally validated in OSLO-COMET with broadly comparable net benefit. Models were implemented in the online tool PLATO (Personalised Liver metastases risk AssessmenT in Oncology). Conclusion: Established CRLM risk scores can be translated into individualised probabilistic recurrence estimates at clinically relevant time points, supporting patient communication, risk-adapted surveillance and transparent benchmarking of next-generation prognostic models.

after.authors: Trius-Soler, M.; da Costa-Seco, T.; Rewers, A.; Cuparencu, C.; Raabyemagle, A. M.; Tetens, I.; Guasch-Ferre, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Copenhagen
after.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide. Diet plays a key role in CVD prevention while linking human health with environmental sustainability. The EAT-Lancet Commission proposed the Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a predominantly plant-based dietary pattern emphasizing high-quality foods and reduced meat consumption. Despite growing interest in the PHD, no randomized controlled trial (RCT) has evaluated its effects using the PHD index on established and novel cardiometabolic biomarkers. Methods: The PlanetDiet study is a six-month, three-arm parallel RCT investigating the effects of sustainable diets on traditional and novel cardiometabolic risk factors in 180 Danish adults aged 45?70 years at high cardiovascular risk. Participants are randomized to a PHD, an ovo-lacto-vegetarian diet, or their habitual diet (control). The primary outcome is changes in a composite cardiometabolic health score, with secondary outcomes including changes in metabolomic and proteomic profiles. Clinical assessments include the analysis of urine, blood, and faecal samples; continuous glucose monitoring; anthropometry and body composition measurements; dietary records; and self-reported questionnaires assessing physical activity, quality of life and dietary acceptance. To support adherence, participants receive four individualized dietary counselling sessions, two group sessions, seasonal food boxes tailored to their assigned diet, and access to a personalized digital application with recipes, individualized timelines, and visit scheduling. Conclusions: PlanetDiet will provide evidence on the effects of sustainable dietary patterns on cardiometabolic health. It will also investigate molecular pathways linking diet to cardiometabolic disease. Ultimately, the study may inform the development of effective, personalized dietary interventions that promote both human and planetary health. Trial registration: Sustainable Diets and Cardiometabolic Health (PlanetDiet): NCT07189676 [ClinicalTrials.gov] [registered before inclusion start; 2025-09-15]; Unique identifier: H-25030722.

after.authors: Attioui, H.; Lacruz-Pleguezuelos, B.; Carrillo de Santa Pau, E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Computational Biology Group. IMDEA Nutrition Institute, Madrid, Spain
after.abstract: This study is part of the AI4Food project, which aims to identify the physiological and behavioral factors influencing weight variation in overweight and obese individuals through integrative analysis of multi-source data. A 30-day crossover intervention was conducted on 93 participants at IMDEA Nutrition Institute, combining a traditional phase (questionnaires, food diaries) and a digital phase (Fitbit Sense Smartwatch, FreeStyle Libre 2 glucose sensor). The collected data encompassed sleep, glucose, skin temperature, nutrition, and gut microbiome information. After rigorous preprocessing and alignment by intervention days, unsupervised clustering, association analysis, and machine learning models were applied to uncover physiological patterns linked to weight dynamics. Results showed greater weight reduction during the digital phase in Group 2, while between-group differences were not significant. Significant associations were observed between nocturnal respiratory rate, skin temperature, and weight variation. Under participant-level five-fold cross-validation, Random Forest models achieved mean accuracies of 64.3% for thermoregulation and 61.7% for glucose phenotype prediction, with RMSSD, restlessness, and nocturnal respiratory rate among the most influential predictors. In contrast, microbiome composition remained almost stable over the short intervention period. These findings support the potential of AI-driven integration of wearable and nutritional data to stratify metabolic phenotypes and advance personalized nutrition strategies in obesity management.

after.authors: IBRAHIM, M.; ALATARE, A. S.; ADEWUNMI, M. O.; ADEYEMO, A. O.; PRECIOUS, D.-O. J.; ADEGOKE, M. O.; ADELEKE, A. O.; AKINDEJI, I. O.
after.author_corresponding_institution: COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES, UNIVERSITY OF ILORIN
after.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Improper refuse disposal remains an environmental health concern in many Nigerian communities. This study assessed knowledge, attitudes and practices relating to refuse disposal among adult residents of Okelele community, Ilorin East Local Government Area, Kwara State, Nigeria. METHODS: A descriptive cross-sectional community-based study was conducted among 180 adults. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, knowledge, attitudes and disposal practices. Descriptive statistics summarised responses, and chi-square tests assessed associations between categorical variables at a 5% significance level. RESULTS: Of 180 respondents, 102 (56.7%) had good knowledge, while 87 (48.3%) had negative attitudes and 99 (55.0%) had poor refuse-disposal practices. Commonly reported practices included incineration (50.6%), disposal into drains (30.6%) and open burning (21.7%). Absence of waste containers (37.2%) and distance to available containers (28.9%) were the leading reported barriers. Knowledge was associated with practice (chi-square=22.122; p<0.001) and attitude (chi-square=8.221; p=0.016); practice was also associated with attitude (chi-square=5.970; p=0.015). CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS FOR TRANSLATION: Despite generally good knowledge, poor disposal practices were common. Improving access to reliable waste-collection infrastructure, alongside community education and enforcement of local waste-management measures, may help translate knowledge into safer practices. Keywords: Solid waste; Waste management; Knowledge; Attitude; Health behavior; Nigeria

after.title: Preprint: Time at the curb, not the rate of head scanning, distinguishes street crossing in virtual reality with severe-to-profound visual impairment
after.authors: Erkat-Cohen, B.; Venugopal, D.; Sadeghi, R.; Tran, C.; Gee, W.; Livingston, B.; Dagnelie, G.; Kartha, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: SUNY College of Optometry
after.abstract: Purpose: We tested whether people with severe-to-profound visual impairment compensate at street crossings with more head scanning and/or more time at the curb. Methods: Ten normally sighted controls, tested with normal vision and with Bangerter filters simulating severe-to-profound visual impairment (approximately 20/2000), and 17 adults with severe-to-profound visual impairment crossed a virtual street in a head-mounted display. Four complexity levels ranged from an empty street to yielding vehicles with pedestrian avatars; only the two most complex levels contained moving vehicles. Cumulative absolute head yaw and latency to step-off were analyzed with mixed-effects models, and latencies were fitted with an ex-Gaussian distribution. Results: Compared with normal vision, latency to step-off was 1.57 times longer with simulated and 1.82 times longer with clinical severe-to-profound visual impairment (Bonferroni p < 0.001 and p = 0.008, respectively). In severe-to-profound visual impairment, the additional latency was attributable to the slow tail of the latency distribution (exponential component {tau} longer by 3.40 s without and 6.20 s with moving vehicles; Bonferroni p = 0.037 and 0.022, respectively); peak position did not differ significantly. Before step-off, cumulative absolute head yaw increased with complexity, F(3, 115.8) = 37.16, p < 0.001, and was 1.88 times higher with simulated impairment than with normal vision (Bonferroni p = 0.024); it did not differ significantly between clinical impairment and normal vision, either before step-off or during walking (both Bonferroni p [≥] 0.479). During walking, its increase with complexity depended on viewing condition, F(6, 109.3) = 5.23, p < 0.001. Conclusions: Severe-to-profound visual impairment was associated with longer and more variable time at the curb, without a significant increase in cumulative head scanning, although the increase in head scanning with complexity during walking was attenuated. Time at the curb is relevant to orientation and mobility practice and accessible crossing design.

after.title: Preprint: Co-Design of the VIRtual physiotherapist-led Triage of referrals to shoUlder surgEons (VIRTUE) model of care: a study protocol
after.authors: Gamble, A. R.; Ferreira, G. E.; Maher, C. G.; Whittle, S.; Avdalis, C.; Harris, I. A.; Langford, A.; Williams, C. M.; Tambree, K.; Hassett, L.; Haynes, A.; Malliaras, P.; Anderson, D. B.; Zadro, J. R.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Musculoskeletal Health, Sydney Local Health District, University of Sydney, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia
after.abstract: Background: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain accounts for up to 85% of shoulder pain. Guidelines recommend 6 months of non-surgical care before considering surgery, yet many are referred to a surgeon before trying it. High referral rates to public hospital shoulder surgery clinics in Australia mean many patients wait 1-2 years to see a surgeon, during which symptoms may become more complex and costly to manage. A promising solution is the VIRtual physiotherapist-led Triage of referrals to shoUlder surgEons (VIRTUE) model of care, in which physiotherapists screen new referrals and determine suitability for non-surgical care or surgical review. However, no such model has been co-designed to incorporate virtual care nor evaluated in a randomised controlled trial. Aims: The broad aim of this study is to co-design the VIRTUE model of care ready for evaluation in a randomised controlled trial conducted in public hospital shoulder surgery clinics in Australia. Specifically, this study has two aims (two stages): i) explore stakeholders perceptions of the feasibility, acceptability and implementation of the VIRTUE model of care for adults with rotator cuff-related shoulder pain who are referred to public hospital shoulder surgery clinics; and ii) co-design the VIRTUE model of care so that it is user-centred and acceptable to patients, clinicians and key stakeholders. Methods: Stage 1 is a qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured online interviews with patients, clinicians and key stakeholders, recruited using purposive, maximum variation sampling. Interviews will explore experiences of current care, perceptions of the proposed model, and barriers and facilitators to implementation, guided by the Theoretical Framework for Acceptability and Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Stage 2 will use Experience-Based Co-Design methodology and involves three online workshops: separate workshops for patients, and for clinicians and key stakeholders, then a combined workshop. Workshops will explore Stage 1 findings, perceptions of the proposed model, and refinements needed to finalise it, with data mapped to the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications-Expanded. Conclusion: Co-designing VIRTUE with patients, clinicians and key stakeholders will ensure it is user-centred, acceptable and feasible within Australian public health services, ready for evaluation in a randomised controlled trial. By facilitating timely and equitable access to evidence-based care, VIRTUE could improve outcomes for patients, ensure specialist services are available for those most in need, and improve health system performance.

after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Pittsburgh
after.abstract: Regulation of complement activity influences immunity and clinical outcomes of SARS-2 CoV-2 infections. Here we investigated antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and complement activity in men (age 36 to 86) and women (age 39 to 83) with (MWH, WWH) and without (MWOH, WWOH) HIV-1. Antibody responses in WWH were lower than in MWH. WWH also had negligible change in blood C3a post-immunization, whereas MWH had greater C3a levels. We investigated the levels of C5, C5a, C1-INH, factor H, and circulating immune complex-C1q (CIC-C1q) binding to understand the regulation of complement activity. We found that C1-INH and anti-S antibody levels were driving the differences in C3 convertase activity in MWH. No significant differences were found between C5 and C5a in both cohorts, suggesting that C5 convertase is not being activated. These results show that biological sex may impact SARS-CoV-2 immune responses and highlights the need for further investigation.

after.authors: Schwabl, P.; Niangaly, A.; Nickols, W.; Callier, V.; Mateja, A.; Kayentao, K.; Ongoiba, A.; Skinner, J.; Preston, A. C.; Doumbo, S.; Doumtabe, D.; Amaya-Romero, J. E.; Kelley, K. after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Immunology and Infectious Diseases, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health; Boston, MA, USA
after.abstract: Early-phase trials of candidate malaria interventions in endemic areas often use "time-to-first" infection as a primary efficacy endpoint. This approach does not assess infection risk after the initial infection, and its censoring of trial participants after their first infection can introduce bias by removing more high-risk participants from control than treatment arms over time. Efficacy estimate precision may also decline as risk set size decreases. Here we assessed the utility of genotyping all infections in an intervention trial to determine the total infection incidence in each participant for the full follow-up period. Specifically, we genotyped all Plasmodium falciparum infections detected in a previously-reported phase 2 trial of the antimalarial monoclonal antibody CIS43LS in 330 Malian adults. We determined the molecular force of infection (molFOI; rate of new P. falciparum strains) for each participant, expressing efficacy as the percent molFOI reduction in CIS43LS versus placebo arms (EffmolFOI). Six-month EffmolFOI was 86.5% (95% CI: 80.1-90.8) and 70.7% (61.0-78.0) for the 40 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg doses, respectively. These estimates are similar to those from time-to-first infection analysis, but more precise when analyzing efficacy by trial-month and when stratifying by P. falciparum infection-status at enrollment. Participants infected at enrollment had lower EffmolFOI and acquired infections earlier in the trial, creating systematic differences in risk composition between arms over time. Genotyping showed no evidence for escape-polymorphisms in the CIS43LS epitope. These results demonstrate how genotypic endpoints can provide a more comprehensive understanding of candidate malaria interventions.
